doc.title: Dave Rivello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Rhythm section parts: written bass and doubling piano
summary: Bass parts are written out, the piano doubles ensemble lines as Brookmeyer and Schneider did, unlike Thad Jones's chord-only charts.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I was watching a YouTube selection, “Beyond the Fall.” I wondered if there’s parts in the piece that don’t necessarily have chord symbols that can be assigned to these four measures or whatever. Are you beyond thinking that way?

Sometimes. In that piece probably there’s moments where the soprano saxophone solo is and those backgrounds are happening and they get more and more dissonant, that it’s just, I think I just labeled it as like whatever area I was in harmonically, like D5. So it was just fifths in the bottom and then I let them try to navigate what all the stuff that’s happening around them once the backgrounds start coming in. Other than that there’s just a lot of sus chords I guess, that could be labelable but in general with my own band the rhythm section parts, there’s often not a lot of chord symbols. The bass parts are written out. Jeff Campbell once said that playing bass in my band was like playing fourth trombone. Because everything is written. There’s not just where they — maybe in a section where there’s soloing there might be in some of the pieces, but other pieces the bass vamp is specifically written. I let the guys — they’ll vary from that and come back to it. And then the piano part is eight or ten fingers of generally doubling what’s going on in the ensemble, so they’re not just sitting there comping. So generally there’s not too much chord symbol stuff in many of my pieces.
Wow. I like the idea of using the piano to double parts too. It definitely gives you a different tone. Not that many people employ it that way.

No it’s true. And with twelve pieces I’ve also then got support under there if I need that. I can use the piano to also help if it’s a large voicing that will help support underneath or I can have them support the trumpets or wherever it is. But I noticed that, well Brookmeyer © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

often had, always in his own band, had a pianist and a synthesizer. And one or the other of them, or both, were doubling different parts of the ensemble. And he got a certain sound by doing that. And Maria Schneider also often times she’ll double the upper voices of, if they’re woodwinds or the trumpets, she’ll have that covered in the piano. So her parts are a lot more notated than say Thad Jones, where it was just the harmonic information, just the chords and the pianist is left on their own kind of to figure out where to play, where not to play, and so it’s a different way of approaching the rhythm section, but I think about it that as a composer I have a lot of — rights sounds like a strong word but I have the right to control the rhythm section and choose what I want them to do, rather than just kind of letting that be their choice. Sometimes I want it to be their choice, because I want to know what they’re going to do there, because that inspires me. But sometimes I want to be sure of exactly what’s going to happen and that’s when I notate what I want to be there.
